courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset
md: Densification is driven by the *positional* gradient, not by the photometric error at a pixel directly. A region can look wrong yet not densify if its Gaussians are not being pushed around, which is one reason poorly observed regions stay blurry.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: One final score hides where the gain came from
md: An ablation turns one end-to-end number into a per-component account: what each stage adds, on the same queries and labels, under the same settings. Without it, you cannot tell which stage earns its latency.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: A common misconception: "the user can only reach this page through a link we show them, so it is protected". The server receives raw HTTP requests. Anyone can type any URL, edit any parameter and replay any request with tools like curl. Hiding a link is not access control.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Multi-tenant isolation: tenant ids everywhere, row-level security
md: Two RLS traps. First, if the app connects as the table owner or a superuser, the policies are silently skipped. Second, with a connection pool (open database connections the app reuses across requests), set the tenant with `set_config(..., true)` or `SET LOCAL` inside the request's transaction so it cannot leak into the next request that reuses the connection.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberos from zero: KDC, tickets, krbtgt and the PAC
md: Kerberos runs on keys derived from passwords. The TGT is locked with krbtgt's key; each service ticket is locked with the key of the account owning the SPN; the PAC inside carries groups and two signatures. Nearly every Kerberos attack is 'get one of those keys' or 'abuse who may ask for which ticket'.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: ACL abuse and attack paths: the directory as a graph
md: AD permissions form a graph of who can control what. Attackers chain small rights into paths to Domain Admins; BloodHound shows the same graph to defenders. Remove the edges into Tier 0, then alert on permission, membership and password-reset changes. To respond, revert the change, reset any account whose password, SPN or RBCD attribute was written, and use 5136 history to find what else that subject changed.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Inside an OLE file: the compound file format by hand
md: Extensions lie in both directions. A file named `.doc` can really be RTF, OOXML, XML or MHTML, and olevba checks the type from the content before parsing. A file named `.txt` can be an OLE file. Always sniff the bytes first.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: Evasion is evidence. A sample that checks for debuggers and virtual machines is telling you it has something to hide. Record every check you find as a behaviour (T1622, T1497) in the report, with the branch it controls.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
md: CFI answers "is this jump allowed?" Data-only attacks never make a disallowed jump. Defences must also protect the data that decisions depend on, and the most complete answer is still not having the memory bug.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: FGSM and PGD: attacking our own toy model
md: FGSM is a quick probe; PGD is the baseline a robustness claim must survive. Always report the norm, epsilon, steps, step size and whether the attack was untargeted or targeted.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Finding backdoors: spectral signatures, filtering and provenance
md: Backdoor defence is layered: provenance and access control keep poisons out, filtering removes most of what gets in, and retraining from versioned clean data is the fallback. No single detector is a guarantee.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
md: Deconfliction protects the organisation, not the red team. Every alert goes through normal escalation; the control group answers "ours or not" from precise operator logs; anything that does not match is a real incident; and the red team pauses when a real intruder may be present.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Regulated red teaming: TIBER-EU, DORA and CBEST
md: Regulated schemes formalise everything in this course: intelligence chooses the adversary, a small control team holds the secret and the stop button, flags define success, leg-ups are logged, every action is recorded, and the test ends in a replay and purple teaming rather than a pass mark.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: A harness is a loop: call the model, run the tool calls it asks for, append the results, repeat until the model returns no tool calls or a budget runs out. Everything else (context management, permissions, traces, evals) is infrastructure around that loop.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
md: Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why intrinsic self-correction often fails
md: Self-correction works when the feedback carries information the generator did not have: a failing test, a compiler error, a schema violation, a human note. Asking the same model to "check again" adds calls, not information.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Direct and indirect injection, and how jailbreaks differ
md: Hidden does not mean exotic. White text, zero-size fonts, HTML comments, alt text, document metadata and invisible Unicode characters are all ordinary ways text reaches a model without a human noticing. If your extractor keeps it, the model reads it.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: RAG and vector stores: poisoning and permission leaks
md: Filtering after the model answers is too late: the model has already read the forbidden chunk and may paraphrase it. Filter before the chunk enters the context, using the same permissions as the source system, kept in sync when they change.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Stability: formation energy and energy above the convex hull
md: The hull test is a 0 K, zero-pressure, ordered-crystal calculation (the Materials Project docs state the 0 K, 0 atm assumption). It ignores entropy, so it can favor artificially ordered arrangements of similar atoms that would be disordered at real synthesis temperatures. "On the hull" means "thermodynamically plausible in DFT", not "can be made in a lab".

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
md: An API key in a mobile app or a web page is public. Anyone can unpack the app and read it. Keys that must stay secret belong on servers; a client that runs on the user's device needs a per-user token instead. Defender view: a fixed prefix like `sk_` lets secret scanners find leaked keys in code; log the key id (never the secret) per request and revoke on any leak.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
md: Changing the password does not reliably remove an app's granted consent. RFC 9700 only says servers *may* revoke refresh tokens on a password change, and the consent record itself stays. Response to consent phishing means finding and revoking the app's consent and tokens, not just resetting credentials.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth
md: In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
md: KEV says "exploited now", EPSS says "likely soon", CVSS says "how bad if it happens", and your inventory says "where, how exposed, how important". Rank by evidence of exploitation and exposure first, severity second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`, a future that returns `Pending` once after arranging its own wakeup, so the scheduler may run something else first.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
md: Hashing is not encryption. If a company can email you your old password, it is stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. A hash with no salt is only slightly better than plaintext against an attacker with a list of common passwords.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
md: A TOTP code proves you hold the shared secret right now. It does not prove which website you are typing it into: anyone who sees the code within its 30-second window can use it once. Lesson 12 exploits exactly that gap.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Beyond classical CAN: CAN FD, CAN XL, LIN, FlexRay and Ethernet
md: Moving from CAN to Ethernet does not by itself add security. Texas Instruments' zone architecture paper warns that "Ethernet-based attack methods and tools common on the internet will be largely applicable to road vehicles". IP inside the car brings IP's attacks (spoofing, scanning, flooding) along with its bandwidth.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Everything here uses an image we built from our own code. Real vendor firmware is often covered by licence terms, and some contains other parties' secrets; analyse only devices and images you own or are authorised to test, and never download firmware to attack devices you do not control.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Does ternary scale? The evidence and its limits
md: Read the scale. The accuracy evidence in the b1.58 paper stops at 3.9B parameters and 100B tokens, plus one 3B model at 2T tokens. Everything larger is a measurement of speed, memory and energy, not of quality.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides
md: Ask of every IPC method: which argument identifies *who is asking*, and does the privileged side get that from its own state or from the message? Identity must come from the browser's state. Everything in the message is attacker input to be range-checked, type-checked and allowlisted.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Who finds browser bugs: bounties, in-the-wild 0-days and practice
md: Across every case in this course the pattern is the same: one bug class (type confusion, use-after-free, a stale check, a trusted value from a less privileged process), one boundary it crossed, and one fix that either corrects the logic or moves the boundary. Defenders win the n-day race by knowing which of their products sit behind which boundary.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: Do not let IT set the MTD by asking "how fast could we restore it?". That gives you the current capability, not the requirement. The BIA asks the process owner "how long until this becomes unacceptable?", and the gap between the two answers is the work of the rest of this course.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Granularity is a recovery requirement. In multi-tenant systems (one data store, many customers), "restore the database" also rolls back every unaffected customer. Write RTOs per restore size (one record, one tenant, many tenants, everything) and test each, because they are different procedures with very different times.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model
md: A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: Misconception: "filler tokens did not help, so all of a model's reasoning must be in the words." Lanham's result shows that particular models did not learn to use filler. Pfau et al. show training can teach a transformer to compute across meaningless tokens on suitable problems, and nothing in a monitor's view of "......" would reveal what was computed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: These methods sit uneasily with "keep optimization pressure off the CoT". VFT trains directly on CoT content. The difference from Baker et al.'s failure is direction and timing: it rewards saying more, before RL, and the RL reward never reads the CoT. VFT was tested on one 8B model with multiple-choice cues; whether it holds for frontier agents is open.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The LLM engine loop: hiding CPU scheduling behind the GPU
md: An engine step is a two-stage pipeline: CPU work and GPU work. Overlap turns the period from their sum into their maximum, CUDA graphs shrink the launch cost inside the GPU stage, and the CPU must never become the larger stage. The price of planning ahead is seeing each token one step late.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
md: "We patched the oracle" is weaker than "we removed RSA key exchange". ROBOT found new oracles in implementations that already had Bleichenbacher countermeasures, because a single timing or TCP behaviour difference is enough.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
md: Security is set by the weakest place a key is accepted and the weakest option a negotiation allows. Give each key one job in one protocol, put the job's name inside everything it signs, and remove options rather than defending them.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: After Van Buren: 'without authorization' asks whether you may enter the system at all; 'exceeds authorized access' asks whether you entered an area your access does not extend to. Motive is not the test. DOJ policy adds: decline good-faith research, and do not charge contract-only theories.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: The exemption itself says it is "not a safe harbor from, or defense to" other laws, naming the CFAA. Circumventing a TPM on someone else's server can be legal under 1201 and still be unauthorised access. And the exemption covers the act of circumvention, not distributing circumvention tools.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: "The IRB said it was not human research" and "no bug was merged" did not end the matter. Ethics review is a floor, like law. If your study manipulates people's behaviour, they are participants, whatever the form says.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Domain weights are not a zero-sum allocation of quality. Because very easy and very noisy domains need few samples, and domains transfer to each other, a better mixture can lower loss on **every** domain at once, including the ones it shrinks.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, clean and filter documents (lesson 9's rules and deduplication, then a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
md: Start every data security question from the data: what is it, where are *all* its copies (including tickets, exports and backups), who can read each one, how can it leave, and when will each copy be destroyed.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
md: Separate owner, application, analyst and admin roles; grant explicit columns or views rather than whole tables; never rely on revoking one column from a table-level grant; and keep grants in version control so drift is visible.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
md: A decoy has no legitimate users, so the number of things that touch it is tiny. That, not cleverness, is where its signal comes from. Every design choice in this course protects that property.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
md: Your own tools will touch decoys: vulnerability scanners, identity-governance jobs that read every account, auditors' scripts, and secret scanners that verify the keys they find (TruffleHog's check calls sts:GetCallerIdentity, which fires a decoy AWS key). List them before go-live and route their hits to a review queue, not to silence. A decoy that a weekly script trips is a decoy everyone learns to ignore.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
md: Protecting the workflow file is not enough. With I-PPE the attacker never touches it: they edit what it calls. Treat everything the privileged job executes (Makefiles, scripts, test files, tool configs, lockfiles) as part of the pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: An estimate of the bound is not the log-probability. d1's one-pass mean-field estimate is biased by construction, and an ELBO estimate is both a bound and noisy. Methods that work here control that error (shared masks, many timesteps, random prompt masks as regularization); plugging a single random ELBO sample into an AR recipe is what LLaDA 1.5 calls naive DPO.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: The KV handoff in detail: protocol, layouts and failures
md: The handoff is a small distributed protocol: metadata through the proxy, one-sided reads of registered memory, a lease kept alive by the consumer's heartbeats, and a failure policy on the consumer. Different parallelism on the two sides multiplies the reads and needs a layout in which each rank's heads are contiguous.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
md: A free MFT record with a resident `$DATA` still contains the old file's bytes. A large file's record holds only runs, and those clusters may already belong to someone else. Always check whether the clusters a deleted record points to are now allocated before trusting the content.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
md: A matching hash proves the evidence did not change. It does not prove your tool read it correctly or that your report is untampered. Validation and independent cross-checks cover that gap.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
md: The weight $\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$ is what makes DPO work. The authors report that a naive version without this weighting (push chosen up, rejected down, equally on every pair) can make the language model degenerate.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: What end-to-end encryption promises, and against whom
md: E2EE protects message content against the network and the server. It does not protect against a compromised device, and by itself it does not hide metadata. Every later lesson either narrows the server's remaining power (keys, membership, metadata) or limits the damage when a device or key is stolen.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Lost and late messages: skipped keys, limits and header encryption
md: Every place a protocol stores state for an attacker-chosen number (skip counts, retries, devices) needs a bound and an expiry. MAX_SKIP is the Double Ratchet's version of that rule.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Many devices per person: Sesame, fan-out and linked-device phishing
md: Every linked device is a full reader of future messages. The device list is the multi-device equivalent of a group member list: if it can change without the user noticing, E2EE quietly includes the attacker.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: The verifier is a **safety** check, not a security review. It proves your program cannot crash or hang the kernel; it does not judge what the program observes. That is why loading tracing programs requires root, or both the CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON capabilities (slices of root's privilege granted on their own: CAP_BPF for loading BPF programs and maps, CAP_PERFMON for tracing).

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Order of operations for edge models: pick an efficient architecture and distill into it, quantize to int8 with per-channel weights, fall back to QAT if accuracy drops, prune only when your runtime benefits, and verify accuracy, latency and peak RAM on the actual device.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
md: Exposure management is attack surface discovery plus judgement plus follow-through: see what the internet sees, tie each item to an owner and to what attackers are exploiting, and verify every fix from the outside.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Cutting after the first correct answer is the most aggressive compression, and it costs accuracy on hard problems. The useful target is 'one solve plus one check', not 'one solve'.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Double decoding and path normalisation
md: This is the opposite of the detection advice in Python for security work, and both are right. When you *search logs*, decode repeatedly until the text stops changing, so you find every disguise. When you *enforce* a rule, decode exactly once and refuse whatever still looks encoded, so no later layer can produce a new meaning after you said yes.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: URL parser differentials: one URL, two hosts
md: A suffix check like `host.endswith("good.example")` is wrong even with a perfect parser: `evilgood.example` passes it. Compare the whole host exactly, or check for a dot boundary (`host == d or host.endswith("." + d)`).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: AMSI in depth: what the scanner sees, and what it cannot
md: AMSI only sees what a host chooses to send. A script engine that does not call AMSI, a program in a language without AMSI integration, or a compiled binary gets no AMSI scan. And AMSI runs inside the same process as the script: code already running there can interfere with it. So AMSI is one layer, and its silence proves nothing.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What kernel sensors cost: CrowdStrike Channel File 291 (July 2024)
md: Kernel sensors trade safety for visibility and tamper resistance. Content updates that the kernel interprets need the same discipline as code: validation that matches the code, bounds checks, and staged rollout with a canary, because a fleet-wide push is a fleet-wide blast radius.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
md: Normalize to an ID, filter on the ID, and keep the raw string for display and debugging. Run the **same** normalizer on queries and on profiles, or the two sides drift apart and matches silently disappear.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
md: Misconception: Entra ID is just Active Directory hosted by Microsoft. It has no domain controllers you can reach, no Group Policy and no Kerberos for cloud apps. Its trust runs on signed tokens over HTTPS, so its attacks are token, consent and policy attacks, not the ticket attacks of the AD course.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
md: Misconception: the breach needed an exotic exploit. Microsoft stated it was not the result of a product vulnerability. A password spray, a missing MFA setting on a test tenant and an over-privileged legacy app were enough. Inventories of tenants and apps are security controls.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
md: Misconception: if the sign-in log shows MFA, the session is the user's. A replayed token carries the MFA claim from the original sign-in. Judge sessions by where and how tokens are used afterwards, especially in non-interactive sign-ins, not by the MFA flag alone.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
md: Misconception: the sign-in log is the record of everything a stolen account did. It records authentication. What the token was used for lives in Graph activity logs, the Unified Audit Log and each service's own logs, and some of those are off or short-lived by default.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
md: An event loop scales because idle connections cost only a kernel watch and a small struct, and readiness is pushed to a ready list instead of scanned. It stays fast only if every callback is short: push disk I/O, DNS and CPU-heavy work to a pool, and split long jobs into chunks.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: A public benchmark score for a model trained on web-scale data is an upper bound on its skill on your queries, not an estimate. Before trusting a gain, ask whether the model, the synthetic training data or the judge (a language model that grades relevance in place of human labelers) could have seen these queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
md: A sandbox does not make a bug less exploitable; it makes successful exploitation worth less, and forces the attacker to find and chain another bug. Put the riskiest code (parsers of untrusted input) in the least privileged process.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy
md: Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
md: A balance loss is not a free **regularizer** (an extra loss term that nudges the model toward some property). Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx
md: Misconception: "Secure Boot means the firmware is trusted." Secure Boot checks what the firmware *loads*. ESET's correction to the LoJax paper says it plainly: Secure Boot is designed against components from outside the SPI flash and would not have stopped an implant inside it.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Trusting the wrong things: PKfail and CVE-2024-7344
md: A signature vouches for who built a program, not for what it does. Any signed boot component that loads code must pass that code back through the platform's verification, or it becomes a hole in the chain for every machine that trusts its signer.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Implementation is implication: the detailed spec, seen through a refinement mapping, must allow only behaviors the abstract spec allows. Extra internal steps are fine because they map to stuttering steps.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Never trust a device signal you did not verify. A header or a JavaScript value is a claim made by the client. Use it to raise suspicion when claims disagree or repeat across many accounts, not to grant trust on its own.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
md: Every promotion is a price per account. Tie it to a scarce identity, check the link between referrer and referee, and hold the payout until the qualifying payment can no longer be reversed.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: Filtering out the 2600 Hz tone would have been a weak fix: phreaks used many other tones, and a filter on a shared channel is always a race. Removing the attacker's access to the control channel ended the whole class of trick.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise
md: Conficker showed both sides of collective defence: an industry coalition could deny a botnet its control channel at internet scale, but cleaning millions of unmanaged PCs was beyond it. Patching (MS08-067 was a month old) and removing risky defaults (AutoRun) would have prevented most infections.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: SolarWinds attacked what you install (a trusted vendor's build), Log4Shell lived in what you import (a free library inside other products). The responses were inventory (SBOMs), verifiable builds, least privilege for powerful tools like network monitors, and review boards that turn incidents into public lessons.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Testing a site's proxies or cache for these bugs can harm *other* users, because the leftover bytes or poisoned entries land on real people. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test, and prefer your own lab: the toys in this course run entirely in one Python process.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
md: A cache key is a promise: "any two requests with this key deserve the same response". Every attack in the next lessons breaks that promise, either because the response depended on something outside the key, or because two different resources ended up under one key.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache (the kernel's in-memory cache of file data) and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: Zones are not VLANs. A VLAN (virtual LAN) is one way to separate traffic, but NIST lists VLANs as logical separation 'when physical separation may not be feasible'. A zone boundary needs an enforcement point, and a misconfigured switch trunk can quietly merge two zones.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: A firewall rule that says 'allow 10.0.0.0/8 to OT, any port, temporary' is the most common way segmentation fails. Review the rule table regularly, expire temporary rules automatically, and alert on hits to rule 11: traffic nobody planned is either a misconfiguration or an intruder.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Inside a SAML response: Issuer, Subject, Conditions and statements
md: Attributes are authorization input. An SP that maps `groups=admins` in the assertion to admin rights hands role decisions to whoever controls assertion content: the IdP's administrators, anyone who compromises them, and anyone who can get an unsigned assertion past the SP.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Conditional access: deciding at sign-in, and what happens after
md: Conditional access decides at the moment of issuance. Everything after that moment is protected by token lifetime, session binding and signals, so a policy is only as strong as the session it produces.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download
md: Disabling the IdP account is not deprovisioning. It blocks the next single sign-on. Sessions already open, tokens already issued, local accounts and shared passwords all survive it.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
md: Measure the tail, not just the median: one leaver with 400 hours of access matters more than a good average. Pair hygiene metrics (orphans, dormant, standing privilege, owners) with detections for terminated logins, out-of-process grants, vault and break-glass use.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: An incident starts when the attacker acts, not when you declare it. The HSE intrusion began on 18 March 2021 and was declared on 14 May. The gap (dwell time) is what your logs, memory and timeline work must reach back across.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Acquisition: memory, disk images, cloud snapshots and logs
md: Encryption changes the plan. If a disk uses BitLocker or another full-disk encryption, an image taken after power-off is unreadable without the recovery key. Capture what you need from the running system, or make sure the key is in your hands before you shut it down.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Threat modelling a device: who can reach it, and how
md: A common mistake is to skip the physical position because "attackers would need the device". Attackers can buy the device. The right question is what one opened unit gives them: its owner's data (acceptable for many products) or a key to all units (never acceptable).

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Medical devices: FDA section 524B, pacemakers and insulin pumps
md: A medical maker cannot ship fixes as casually as a phone maker: each change may need risk review, and an implant update happens in a clinic. That is why FDA expects the update path and the postmarket plan to be designed before approval, not invented after a disclosure.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal
md: Misconception: "since 2016 only Microsoft-signed drivers load." Only *new* drivers had to go through Microsoft. Drivers already signed under the cross-signing program, with leaf certificates from before 29 July 2015, kept loading on most systems for a decade. Many drivers later abused in BYOVD attacks date from that era.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Kernel Data Protection and PatchGuard: guarding data, catching patches
md: Misconception: "PatchGuard makes kernel tampering impossible." Microsoft's own description is narrower: it detects certain modifications and shuts the system down, and it does not prevent all malware. In the BlackByte case, Sophos reported that security callbacks were removed regardless. Treat KPP as a tripwire, not a wall.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Hints match a teacher layer through a learned regressor; attention transfer sums channels away so widths need not match; TinyBERT matches attention matrices and hidden states layer by layer through a mapping g(m); DistilBERT aligns last-layer directions with a cosine loss.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes, more hits: KV compression and non-prefix reuse
md: Compression lowers the break-even bandwidth by the compression ratio, which can turn a slow tier from useless to worth reading. Position-independent reuse turns reordered RAG chunks into hits. Both trade a little accuracy, so measure answer quality, not only TTFT.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
md: Read the theorem for what it is: a construction showing a 2-layer model with continuous thoughts *can* solve reachability in D steps, using embeddings as wide as the vocabulary. It does not show that a pretrained LLM learns this on GSM8k, and the matching experiments are small models trained from scratch on graph tasks.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
md: Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop
md: A baseline you apply once decays. Write it down, apply it with an idempotent tool on a schedule, scan for drift, and stream telemetry off every host. The rest of this course fills in each box of that loop.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record
md: Audit records come from the kernel, not the program, and one event is several records sharing TIME:SERIAL. auid (the login uid) is set once at login and survives su and sudo, which is what lets you attribute root actions to a person.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: Tetragon filters in the kernel and can act there. Hook LSM functions such as security_file_permission rather than raw system call arguments, start in observe mode, and pair Sigkill with Override when the operation itself must not happen.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable does not mean uncompromisable. A remote bug still gives an attacker code execution in memory until the next reboot, and writable areas still persist. Keep runtime telemetry; immutability shrinks persistence, not intrusion.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
md: An evaluator is a measuring instrument. Before trusting any number it produces, check how often it agrees with careful human judgment on your task, at the level (single output or whole system) at which you will use it.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
md: Read the coverage notes, not just the feature list. Per the AWS docs, sensitive information filters do not mask PII the model writes into tool call arguments, and grounding checks on a streamed response (one sent to the user piece by piece as it is generated) may mark it irrelevant only after it has been streamed. A guardrail protects only the channels it actually inspects.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a prompt: rules, delimited inputs and the task
md: A good prompt separates three things the model must not confuse: the rules (stable), the input data (fenced in tags), and the task (stated plainly, ideally last). Then measure: every vendor guide says prompting is iterative and should be checked against test cases.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
md: The `minimum_should_match` default depends on context. In Elasticsearch it is 1 only when the bool has `should` clauses and no `must` or `filter` clauses; otherwise it is 0, and the should clauses become optional score boosts. Put Berlin and remote as bare should clauses next to a filter list and *every* city passes.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: Output tokens are the expensive kind for latency. Prefer designs whose answer is one token or one logit: pointwise labels, PRP in scoring mode, or FIRST-style first-token ranking.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
md: Pick the formulation by its failure mode: pointwise needs calibration, pairwise needs many calls, listwise needs a long context and a good initial order. Most practical gains come from controlling those failure modes (swapping, shuffling, cascades, distillation), not from a cleverer single prompt.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates.
